memory_candidates.content: When testing destructive or concurrency-sensitive shell script changes (locks, mutexes, status writers) against a live, shared, actively-used state file (e.g. a task tracker's state.json), never test against the real record you are yourself part of. Add a disposable scratch row via a targeted jq read-modify-write (never a wholesale file overwrite, which risks clobbering a concurrent session's simultaneous write), run the real tests against that scratch row, then remove it via a targeted jq del() -- also never a wholesale overwrite. If a test accidentally mutates or deletes a real, live lock/record (e.g. an unconditional 'release' call hitting the wrong target), restore it immediately with the correct values before continuing, and treat the mistake as a signal to isolate further testing onto disposable scratch data.

When ambient system load (e.g. several concurrent sibling agent sessions) makes wall-clock-based regression tests unreliable -- a previously-fast operation measuring orders of magnitude slower under load, unrelated to the change under test -- replace an absolute before/after timing comparison with a load-independent A/B comparison: run the identical contended scenario twice, once with the fix/guard active and once without, under the SAME ambient load, and compare the two runs directly. This isolates the change's actual effect (e.g. a mutex guard eliminating a multi-second contention wait) from noise that would otherwise make a single before/after wall-clock delta meaningless.

In bash, only the LAST-installed 'trap ... EXIT' for a given script is active -- a second trap install silently clobbers the first rather than composing with it. When a script already has an EXIT trap (e.g. for tmp-file cleanup) and a change needs an additional cleanup action to fire on every exit path (e.g. releasing a mutex), extend the existing trap function's body rather than installing a second trap. Make the added action idempotent (guard it behind an 'did I acquire and not yet release' flag) so that if it is ALSO invoked explicitly at the natural end of the critical section, the trap-fired duplicate at script exit is a safe no-op rather than a double-release bug.
